How seven payment gateways stack up for Nigerian businesses
Nigeria’s booming electronic payments market is forcing businesses to think beyond simply accepting money online as the choice of payment
Royal Ibeh
September 15, 2026
7 min read
Listen to this article
Share
Nigeria’s booming electronic payments market is forcing businesses to think beyond simply accepting money online as the choice of payment gateway increasingly affects transaction costs, settlement speed, reliability and the ability to reach customers at home and abroad.
The scale of the market shows why that choice matters. Nigeria Inter-Bank Settlement System Plc (NIBSS) processed more than 11.2 billion instant-payment transactions valued at over N1.07 quadrillion in 2024, while the Central Bank of Nigeria recorded about N3.46 quadrillion in electronic payments across nearly 48 billion transactions in 2025.
Read also: MTN’s 100m subscribers open data, fintech opportunity
With the CBN’s Payments System Vision 2028 also positioning Nigeria as a regional payments hub, competition among payment infrastructure providers is increasingly shifting from basic payment acceptance to scale, speed, connectivity, security and cross-border capability.
For businesses, that means the gateway with the lowest headline fee is not necessarily the cheapest or most suitable option. Settlement time, payment success rates, available channels, integration requirements and access to broader financial infrastructure can have a bigger effect on the cost of doing business.
Seven major providers illustrate the different strategies now competing for Nigerian merchants: Paystack, Monnify, Flutterwave, Interswitch, Squad, Nomba and Paga.
Paystack combines simplicity with scale
Paystack remains one of the strongest options for businesses seeking a relatively straightforward route into online payments.
The company charges 1.5 percent plus N100 for local transactions, capped at N2,000, while the N100 component is waived for transactions below N2,500. International transactions attract a 3.9 percent fee plus N100.
Settlement is generally the next business day. Founded in 2015 and acquired by Stripe in 2020, Paystack has built its position partly around ease of onboarding and developer-friendly integration. It has more than 200,000 merchants and supports cards, bank transfers, USSD, QR codes, Apple Pay, mobile money and payment links.
Its scale also provides an indication of market penetration. Paystack processed N1 trillion in a single month in July 2024, becoming the first Nigerian gateway to reach that level.
For businesses, its attraction is less about having the cheapest price and more about combining a mature developer experience, multiple payment channels, fraud controls and access to Stripe’s global technology ecosystem.
Monnify leans on banking infrastructure
Monnify competes differently, using its connection to TeamApt and the wider Moniepoint ecosystem to emphasise payment infrastructure and settlement.
It charges 1.5 percent on local transactions, capped at N2,000, and four percent on international transactions. Its headline differentiator is settlement, which is offered instantly.
Monnify processed about N25 trillion in transaction value in 2025, equivalent to roughly $18 billion, representing a 38 percent increase from 2023. It has more than 100,000 merchants across 27 Nigerian banks.
The platform offers virtual accounts, payment links, cards, bank transfers, USSD, direct debit, offline payments and disbursements.
That makes it particularly relevant to businesses that need more than a checkout page. Companies collecting money at scale can use virtual accounts and other payment infrastructure to manage flows across different customer and business segments.
Flutterwave offers the broadest cross-border proposition
Flutterwave’s biggest advantage is geographic reach. The company operates across more than 30 countries and supports payments in more than 30 currencies, giving Nigerian businesses selling into other African markets or international markets an infrastructure advantage.
Its customer base includes major global companies such as Uber, Microsoft, MTN and Wise. The trade-off is cost. Local transactions attract a two percent fee, capped at N2,000, following an increase from 1.4 percent in April 2025. International transactions cost 4.8 percent.
For a purely domestic business processing large volumes, that pricing can make cheaper gateways more attractive. For an exporter, digital business or company collecting from customers across multiple markets, however, the additional cost can be justified by the broader payment network.
Flutterwave supports cards, bank transfers, USSD, mobile money, NQR, eNaira and other payment methods.
Interswitch offers institutional depth
Interswitch is the oldest provider in the group, having been founded in 2002, and its competitive advantage is the depth of its financial infrastructure rather than startup-style simplicity.
Its WebPAY product charges 1.5 percent for local transactions, capped at N2,000, with a N150,000 one-time setup fee. International transactions attract 3.5 percent, while settlement is generally the next day.
The company processed 1.2 billion transactions in March 2023 alone, demonstrating the scale of the infrastructure behind its business.
Its ecosystem includes the Verve card scheme, Quickteller and a network of more than 11,000 ATMs.
For large organisations that prioritise institutional relationships, proven infrastructure and deep integration with the Nigerian financial system, that history can be more important than the absence of a setup fee.
For smaller businesses, however, the N150,000 setup cost can make other gateways easier to adopt.
Squad brings banking relationships into the gateway market
Squad, the payments business of HabariPay and part of GTCO, brings another banking-led model to the market.
The company processed N27.4 trillion in transaction value in 2024, putting it among the higher-volume payment platforms operating in Nigeria.
Unlike several competitors, Squad does not publicly list a standard transaction fee in the information available for comparison, making direct price comparisons more difficult.
Its proposition is built around access to GTCO’s banking ecosystem, while its payment tools include cards, bank transfers, USSD, virtual accounts, payment links and soft POS.
That combination gives businesses the ability to connect online and offline collections through a single platform. Its appeal is therefore likely to be strongest for businesses that value banking relationships and integrated payment infrastructure alongside the gateway itself.
Nomba competes aggressively on price
Nomba has one of the clearest cost propositions among the seven. Its local transaction fee is 1.4 percent, capped at N1,800, while international transactions cost 3.9 percent. Businesses processing at least N50 million monthly can also negotiate volume discounts.
The company has more than 600,000 merchants and processes more than N3 trillion in monthly transaction value.
That scale reflects Nomba’s roots in physical merchant payments. The company, formerly known as Kudi, has expanded from agent and point-of-sale services into a broader payments platform combining physical and digital commerce.
Its recent expansion includes Apple Pay on physical POS terminals and a partnership with UK open-banking platform Volume to enable Nigerian merchants to collect pounds directly from UK bank accounts.
For high-volume domestic merchants, its lower fee and N1,800 cap can be significant. A business processing millions of naira every month can see small differences in transaction charges accumulate into substantial costs.
Paga’s advantage is reach beyond digital-first customers
Paga occupies a different part of the market. Founded in 2009 and licensed by the CBN as a mobile money operator, the company combines digital payments with a large agent network.
Its account-funding service is free, while local card transactions attract a 1.5 percent fee. International transactions cost 3.5 percent, with settlement ranging from real time to the next day.
Paga supports mobile money, bank transfers, cards, USSD and wallet payments. Its physical distribution network gives it an advantage among businesses whose customers are not entirely digital-first, particularly those serving rural markets, informal businesses and customers who rely heavily on mobile money.
For such businesses, reach can matter more than having the lowest online transaction fee.
The choice is increasingly about fit
The comparison shows that Nigeria’s payment gateway market is no longer a simple contest over transaction charges.
Read also: CBN tells banks, fintechs to treat cyber risk as financial stability threat
Paystack’s strength is its combination of ease of use, technology and scale. Monnify competes on banking infrastructure and settlement. Flutterwave is strongest where cross-border payments matter. Interswitch brings institutional depth, while Squad leverages banking relationships. Nomba combines aggressive pricing with physical and digital payments, and Paga differentiates itself through its agent and mobile-money reach.
For a small online business, a gateway with simple integration and no setup fee may be the logical starting point. A large merchant may care more about volume pricing, transaction reliability and settlement. A company selling across Africa may accept higher fees in exchange for multi-currency infrastructure, while a business serving less-bankable customers may value agent and wallet networks.
The broader lesson is that payment infrastructure is becoming a strategic business decision rather than a back-office utility.
As Nigeria’s electronic payments market expands, businesses that compare gateways on the full cost and capability of moving money, not just the percentage displayed on a pricing page, will be better positioned to reduce payment friction, improve cash flow and scale.
Data sources: CBN, NIBSS, individual payment gateway pricing pages and company disclosures. Fees and product terms may change, and businesses should verify current charges and settlement conditions directly with providers before making a decision.

Top 10 B2B Fintech Businesses In Nigeria
By
Partner
16th Jun, 2026
Get TC updates in your Newsfeed
Source: TechCabal
Share
Share
The landscape of Nigeria’s business fintech space is highly competitive, with millions of business owners and high-scaling teams constantly looking for platforms to optimise their daily operations.
Fintech has developed over time from basic money transfers to a whole financial infrastructure, assisting businesses with payment support, operational management, and the removal of payment bottlenecks.
Some of the most cutting-edge systems created especially to maintain the efficient operation of corporate budgets are being introduced in 2026. The top ten business fintech platforms in Nigeria at the moment are as follows:
1. Platnova Business
Platnova Business addresses the one problem most Nigerian companies don’t talk about enough: the daily friction of managing multi-currency cash flow through legacy banking infrastructure never built for cross-border operations.
Businesses are provided with dedicated NGN, USD, GBP, and EUR wallets at the click of a button across departments with Platnova Business, without the hassle of multiple correspondent banking relationships or the need to reconcile FX conversions manually. Their global card infrastructure offers configurable spend limits, controlled merchant acceptance, and clean developer API documentation for businesses looking to grow and scale. The outcome is a fully automated spend workflow that, for any scaling business in 2026, is less of a nice-to-have and more of a competitive requirement.
2. Moniepoint Business
Moniepoint is the backbone of physical commerce in Nigeria. Their POS terminals dominate storefronts from Lagos Island to Kano, backed by high uptime, instant settlements, and built-in payroll and inventory tools. For SMEs processing high-volume in-person transactions, Moniepoint remains the most battle-tested option on the market.
3. Paystack (by Stripe)
Paystack operates primarily as an online payment gateway for websites and mobile applications. Their service relies on providing standard developer APIs and documentation for businesses needing card, transfer, or mobile money checkout setups. Recently, the company expanded its scope beyond digital processing by utilizing a microfinance banking license to offer business accounts, structured deposits, and compliance tracking directly through its dashboard
4. OPay Business
OPay’s consumer network feeds directly into its merchant ecosystem, and that’s a more significant advantage than it sounds. A sprawling agent banking network, 99.9% transaction uptime, and zero-fee intra-wallet transfers make OPay Business a serious option for high-volume retail merchants where processing speed and low transaction overhead aren’t negotiable.
5. Flutterwave
Flutterwave operates at an enterprise scale and also functions primarily as an international payment gateway connecting African merchants to global networks. Their platform provides processing across multiple currencies and countries simultaneously, serving businesses that handle cross-border customer collections. Earlier this year, the company secured a local microfinance banking license in Nigeria to internalize elements of its payout chain and speed up merchant settlements.
6. Kuda Business
Kuda has evolved from a consumer neobank into a functional workspace tool for digital-first teams and freelancers. Zero-maintenance business accounts, granular spending analytics, and internal invoicing tools give smaller teams clear cash flow visibility without the operational overhead of traditional corporate banking.
7. Remita
Remita operates as a major transaction processor managing backend payment flows for large-scale operations. Over 150,000 businesses and hundreds of financial institutions use its setup to process corporate payroll, taxes, pensions, and automated collections. Holding licenses from the CBN for payment switching and super-agent services, the platform handles significant volume by bridging public and private sector payment networks
8. Grey Business
Grey built its reputation solving the foreign account problem for Nigerian professionals, and that same infrastructure powers their business product. For remote-first agencies, tech startups, and creator-led businesses billing international clients regularly, Grey’s dedicated foreign virtual accounts with competitive FX conversion rates offer a cleaner alternative to routing payments through traditional correspondent banking.
9. BudPay
BudPay provides standard online payment gateways and payout APIs for digital setups and early-stage companies. Their service focuses on handling local card processing and cross-border transfers without heavy setup requirements
10. PalmPay Business
PalmPay’s real asset is its user base of tens of millions of active wallet holders representing real, accessible purchasing power for consumer-facing merchants. Combined with reliable POS settlement and instant transaction processing, PalmPay is a smart acquisition channel for retail businesses trying to capture Nigeria’s mobile-first commerce market
The infrastructure exists. The question is whether you’re using the right one. Every platform here solves a specific problem. Moniepoint owns in-store payments. Paystack owns the online checkout. Flutterwave handles large cross-border volume transactions. Platnova Business was built to handle developer APIs and documentation, multi-currency wallets, automated spending controls, global cards, and cross-border settlement in a single platform.

Best Business Payment Gateways in Nigeria (2026)
Here are the Best Business Payment Gateways in Nigeria, ranked for SMEs & Founders. This list maps each gateway to the business it is actually designed for
Oluwadamilola Koya
13 min read · Updated October 29, 2026
Save
Follow
Reviewed by Oluwadamilola Koya · June 15, 2026
Jump to Introduction: The Payment Gateway Decision Nobody Takes Seriously Enough Fee Comparison: The All-In View The Full Rankings 1  Paystack 
A A
Save

Advertisement
Advertisement
90 px
Best Business Payment Gateways in Nigeria (2026): Ranked for SMEs & Founders
QUICK ANSWER
Best for startups and e-commerce: Paystack — simplest integration, best developer docs, trusted by 60,000+ businesses. Start here.
Best for cross-border and multi-currency: Flutterwave — 150+ currencies, pan-African reach, $31B processed in 2024. Know the history.
Best for bank transfer-heavy B2B businesses: Monnify — virtual accounts, automated reconciliation, Moniepoint reliability.
Best for fintech builders needing API-first plus stablecoin: Fincra — $10B+ processed, fiat and crypto rails from one integration.
Best for enterprise and government: Remita — the backbone of Nigerian federal salary and institutional payments.
Best for businesses already with GTBank: Squad — deep banking integration, competitive fees, reliable settlement.
Introduction: The Payment Gateway Decision Nobody Takes Seriously Enough
Every Nigerian business that decides to accept online payments makes the same mistake at least once: it picks a gateway based on what other founders are using and discovers six months later that it was built for a different type of business. The startup that picked Paystack for its clean checkout later realized that 70% of its customers prefer bank transfer, and Monnify's virtual account reconciliation would have saved ten hours of monthly admin. The B2B company that chose Flutterwave for its brand cachet discovers it is paying 2% per transaction on invoices where Monnify would have charged 1.4%.
Nigeria's payment gateway market has matured to the point where the right answer genuinely depends on your business model. Paystack and Flutterwave are the names every founder knows. But the conversation in 2026 includes some newer players than you'd usually think! This ranking maps each gateway to the business it is actually designed for.
All fees verified at time of publication — June 2026. Payment gateway fees change frequently and vary by payment method, transaction volume, and negotiated agreements. Confirm current pricing with each provider before integrating.
Fee Comparison: The All-In View
The table below captures headline transaction fees. The real cost is always higher once you account for the specific payment method, currency, and settlement timing you actually use. Read it as a starting point, not a final answer.
Fees confirmed at time of publication. Always verify current rates directly with providers as they shift with CBN directives and business volume negotiations.
The Full Rankings
1 Paystack
60,000+ businesses · Stripe-backed · Best developer docs in Nigeria
Best for Startups, Digital Commerce, and Any Business Going Live Fast
Paystack was founded in Lagos in 2015 and acquired by Stripe for over $200 million in 2020. That acquisition matters in a way that is still playing out: Stripe invested not just money but engineering standards, documentation culture, and global compliance infrastructure into a Nigerian payment company. The result is visible in the product. Paystack's developer documentation is the best -maintained in the Nigerian market. A competent developer can go from zero to live checkout in a day. The webhook and API reliability is consistent. The dashboard is clean enough that non-technical founders can manage their payments without needing a developer for every adjustment.
For a startup or SME that wants to start collecting payments online without a procurement process, Paystack is the fastest, lowest-friction path. No setup fees. A 1.5% + ₦100 per transaction structure that is affordable for early-stage businesses. Support for debit cards, bank transfers, USSD, and Apple Pay; which covers effectively every Nigerian customer's preferred payment method. Payment links that work even without a website.
The payment link feature deserves specific mention: businesses with no website, no app, and no developer can generate a payment link from the Paystack dashboard in seconds and share it via WhatsApp, Instagram, or email. For the wave of Nigerian SMEs that sell primarily through social media, this single feature has been more valuable than the entire Stripe-grade checkout infrastructure.
The honest limitations
At higher transaction values, Paystack's structure can cost more than alternatives. A ₦500,000 invoice processed through Paystack costs ₦7,600 (1.5% + ₦100). The same invoice through Monnify costs ₦7,100 (1.4%, capped at ₦2,000) — a small difference per transaction that compounds meaningfully for businesses doing serious B2B volume. Paystack is also fundamentally card-and-checkout-first in its product DNA. For businesses where the majority of customers pay by bank transfer — which in Nigeria, particularly for high-value B2B transactions, is most businesses; Monnify's infrastructure is more purpose-built.
Who should use Paystack: Startups, e-commerce stores, digital product sellers, subscription businesses, service providers, and any company that wants to be live accepting payments within 24 hours. If you are not sure which gateway to start with, start with Paystack and migrate when your transaction pattern tells you something more specific is needed.
2 Flutterwave
$31B processed 2024 · 150+ currencies · 34 African markets
Best for Cross-Border Commerce and Pan-African Businesses — Know the History
Flutterwave processed $31 billion in transaction value in 2024. That number settles one question permanently: at scale, across Africa and internationally, Flutterwave works. Over a million businesses use it. Uber, Netflix, and Flutterwave's African merchant base process payments through its infrastructure daily. For a Nigerian business with genuine pan-African or international ambitions — accepting payments from Ghana, Kenya, Côte d'Ivoire, South Africa, and the UK simultaneously — Flutterwave is the only local-origin gateway that handles all of those corridors from a single integration.
The multi-currency capability is the product's clearest differentiator. 150+ currencies. PayPal integration. Mobile money across Africa. USSD. Cards. POS. The Flutterwave Store allows businesses with no website to sell globally. The Rave checkout is configurable for complex payment flows. The acquired Mono open-banking infrastructure (January 2026) adds account verification and bank data capabilities that no other gateway in this list currently offers.
The history you need to know before deciding
Flutterwave has accumulated a significant regulatory and governance record since 2022 that any business integrating it should understand before making the decision. The Kenyan Asset Recovery Agency froze $52 million in Flutterwave-linked accounts in 2022 on money laundering suspicions; charges later dropped by the ARA for lack of evidence. In early 2023, a court-documented security breach resulted in approximately $24 million in unauthorised POS transactions. In April 2024, a further breach led to reportedly $7.2 million in illicit transfers. In July 2025, Flutterwave cut roughly 50% of staff in Kenya and South Africa as part of a restructuring. Multiple allegations of workplace harassment and governance failures have accompanied these operational issues.
The full picture: Flutterwave's scale and market position make it, in the words of multiple fintech analysts, 'almost too big to fail.' Its client base and infrastructure are too embedded in African commerce for the platform to simply disappear. But the governance and security record means that any business integrating Flutterwave should do so with eyes open, monitoring for service disruptions, maintaining a fallback gateway, and not treating Flutterwave's continued operation as guaranteed.
The verdict on whether to use Flutterwave is a business decision, not a moral one. If you need pan-African multi-currency payment acceptance, Flutterwave's infrastructure capabilities are genuinely unmatched in the local-origin market. If you operate primarily within Nigeria with Nigerian customers paying in naira, Paystack's cleaner governance record and more focused product may suit you better.
Who should use Flutterwave: Businesses with cross-border or pan-African payment needs. E-commerce platforms accepting multiple African currencies. Companies needing PayPal integration or multi-currency checkout. Integrate with a fallback gateway and maintain awareness of its operational track record.
3 Monnify
Moniepoint subsidiary · Owns CBN switching licence · Lowest effective B2B fees
Best for Bank Transfer-Heavy Businesses — Virtual Accounts and Automated Reconciliation
Most Nigerian customers, particularly for high-value transactions, prefer bank transfer over card. This is not a demographic quirk; it is a rational response to years of card failure rates, fraud exposure, and the simple reliability of bank-to-bank transfer in a market where NIBSS bank transfers rarely fail. Monnify is the gateway that was built around this reality rather than imported from a card-first global template.
Monnify is Moniepoint's payment gateway product, and it inherits Moniepoint's core competency: making bank transfer flows work reliably at scale. The product that makes it genuinely different from Paystack and Flutterwave is the virtual account infrastructure. Monnify assigns dedicated virtual bank account numbers to individual customers or transactions, allowing incoming bank transfers to be automatically matched and reconciled without a human touching a spreadsheet. For businesses processing dozens or hundreds of bank transfers dail: schools collecting fees, B2B platforms receiving invoices, lending companies receiving loan repayments, this automation is worth more than any headline fee comparison.
Pricing: 1.5% per local transaction, capped at ₦2,000. Foreign card transactions attract an extra 3.8% charge. Settlement next-day. Monnify owns a CBN switching licence (one of only two Nigerian payment companies to hold one alongside Interswitch) which reduces its own processing costs and translates into pricing that is competitive without sacrificing margin sustainability.
Monnify's parent Moniepoint processes over 800 million monthly transactions and has achieved unicorn status. The infrastructure reliability that made Moniepoint Nigeria's most trusted POS provider is the same infrastructure Monnify runs on. For businesses where payment failure during a peak period is genuinely costly, that backstop matters.
The honest limitations
Monnify's developer documentation, while functional, does not match Paystack's polish. Non-technical business owners will find the integration less intuitive. The brand is less recognisable to end customers, which occasionally creates checkout trust friction. And for businesses that primarily process card payments from consumers: e-commerce, digital subscriptions, Paystack's consumer-facing checkout experience is more developed.
Who should use Monnify: Fintechs, lending platforms, schools, B2B service businesses, marketplaces, and any company where bank transfers are the primary inbound payment method. If you find yourself manually reconciling bank transfers every month, Monnify's virtual account infrastructure is the solution that should have been in place from day one.
4 Fincra
$10B+ processed · IMTO-licensed · Fiat and crypto rails
Best for API-First Products and Fintech Builders Needing Fiat Plus Stablecoin
Fincra launched in 2021 with an explicit mandate that most Nigerian payment companies have not attempted: build a payment infrastructure that works across African borders at the API level, simultaneously on fiat and stablecoin rails. Between 2023 and 2024, it processed over $10 billion in transaction value, less than Flutterwave by an order of magnitude, but enough to establish production-grade reliability across its corridors.
The distinguishing feature for developers building payment-intensive products is Fincra's dual-rail architecture. The same API handles fiat pay-ins and pay-outs (payment gateway, payment links, permanent virtual accounts, bulk disbursements) as well as stablecoin-settled transactions. For a Nigerian fintech building a product that involves cross-border settlements, a payroll platform, an e-commerce marketplace, and a business banking product, the ability to settle via USDT or USDC alongside naira bank transfers from a single integration eliminates the need for a separate crypto payment infrastructure.
Fincra holds an IMTO license from the CBN, enabling it to process international money transfers, not just domestic payments. That license distinguishes it from gateways that handle naira-to-naira flows only and positions it as a complete cross-border payment infrastructure rather than a local checkout product.
The honest limitations
Fincra is a developer-first product. Non-technical businesses will struggle to integrate it without engineering support. The brand is less well known to end customers than Paystack or Flutterwave, which occasionally creates checkout trust friction. For businesses that do not need stablecoin rails or IMTO-level cross-border capability, Paystack or Monnify offer more purpose-fit solutions.
Who should use Fincra: Fintech startups building payment products that span multiple African countries. Companies that need both fiat bank transfers and stablecoin settlements from a single API. Developer teams building anything that requires IMTO-licensed cross-border transfers alongside domestic naira flows.
5 Interswitch / Quickteller Business
Nigeria's foundational payment infrastructure · 25+ years · 1.2B transactions
Best for Established Businesses with Traditional Banking Depth

Interswitch has been building Nigerian payment infrastructure since 2002. The Verve card — Nigeria's dominant domestic payment card — is an Interswitch product. The switching infrastructure that underpins most Nigerian bank transactions passes through Interswitch's rails. This is not a company disrupting a market. It is the market's original layer, and it has been there long enough that every major Nigerian bank has deep technical integration with its systems.
For established businesses with existing bank relationships and institutional clients, Interswitch's breadth of bank connectivity and Verve card processing is a practical advantage that newer entrants cannot simply claim. The setup cost — approximately ₦150,000 — and one to two-week onboarding timeline are appropriate for companies with procurement processes rather than startups that need to be live today. The developer experience is less polished than Paystack, but the institutional reliability track record is longer.
Who should use Interswitch: Established businesses in retail, hospitality, and enterprise services where deep bank integration, Verve card acceptance, and institutional credibility matter. Not suited for early-stage startups that need speed of integration.
6 Remita
Nigeria's salary payment backbone · Federal government infrastructure
Best for Enterprise, Payroll, and Government-Adjacent Businesses
Remita is how the Nigerian federal government pays salaries. It is how government agencies collect fees, universities collect tuition, and parastatals manage payroll disbursements. That is not a feature claim; it is an operational description of the system millions of Nigerians interact with as employees and students without necessarily knowing the name behind it.
For private sector businesses outside the government ecosystem, Remita's institutional DNA can feel bureaucratic. The integration complexity is higher than that of Paystack. The pricing is negotiated rather than published transparently. The product roadmap reflects institutional needs first. But in the specific niche it dominates (large-scale institutional payment collection and salary disbursement), Remita has no peer. If your business sells to government agencies, educational institutions, or manages payroll for large employee populations, Remita is not optional.
Who should use Remita: Companies with government or institutional clients. Schools, universities, and hospitals are collecting fees at scale. Businesses managing payroll disbursements for large employee bases. Any company where government payment infrastructure is a contractual requirement, not a choice.
7 Squad (GTBank)
GTBank fintech arm · Banking infrastructure integration · Competitive fees
Best for Businesses Already Within the GTBank Ecosystem
Squad is GTBank's fintech payment product, and it inherits something that no standalone gateway can replicate: the deepest possible integration with one of Nigeria's most recognised commercial banks. For businesses that bank with GTBank, particularly those that want tight payment-to-settlement workflows, or whose customer base has high GTBank card ownership, Squad offers an integration that feels native rather than layered on top.
The fee structure is competitive, the settlement times are reliable, and the GTBank brand provides checkout credibility that newer gateways are still building. The limitation is that Squad's advantages are most pronounced for businesses already inside the GTBank ecosystem. For businesses that bank elsewhere or serve customers across multiple banks, Paystack or Monnify will offer more breadth with less friction.
What Nigerian Businesses Get Wrong About Payment Gateways
The most expensive mistake is choosing a gateway based on brand recognition and discovering six months later that your transaction pattern, high-value bank transfers, international customers, subscription billing, required a gateway with different architectural strengths. Before choosing, map your actual payment flows in writing: what do your customers pay with? In what currencies? What volume do you expect? Do you need automated reconciliation?
The second mistake is single-gateway dependency. Every payment gateway experiences downtime. Nigeria's payment infrastructure experiences periods of instability beyond any gateway's control. The businesses that process significant volume should maintain a primary and a fallback gateway. The conversion rate improvement from fewer payment failures during a competitor's outage quickly pays for the second integration.
The third, underrated mistake: ignoring the settlement cutoff time. Next-day settlement is standard across most gateways listed here, but 'next day' has a cutoff, typically 4 pm. Transactions processed after that cutoff may not settle until the following business day. Friday afternoon payments may not settle until Monday. For businesses managing payroll, rent, or supplier payments against a tight cash flow timeline, the actual settlement calendar, not just the headline policy, is a number you should know before you integrate.

Nigeria Fintech in 2026: OPay, Moniepoint, PalmPay, Kuda and the Market Map
Nigeria is Africa's most funded fintech market and its most demanding one. Two unicorns are preparing for public markets, the regulator has handed the largest players national licences, and the naira has rewritten every dollar valuation. This is where the market stands, company by company, with the figures sourced.
MobiBank Editorial
·
October 9, 2026
·
12 min read
The short answer
Nigerian fintech in 2026 is a market of a few very large agent and merchant networks, now regulated like banks and heading for listings.
OPay is implied at around $3.1 billion by its shareholder Opera and is reported to be exploring a US listing near $4 billion. Moniepoint is a unicorn that raised a $200 million Series C. PalmPay is reported to be raising at a valuation above $1 billion with a Hong Kong listing in view. Kuda cut its losses by 84% in 2024. In January 2026 the Central Bank of Nigeria upgraded all of them to national microfinance licences.
For an investor, Nigeria is two stories at once. The demand side is enormous and still growing: tens of millions of adults moving from cash to digital payments, a payments system processing quadrillions of naira, and remittances above $21 billion a year. The supply side is consolidating fast, around a handful of operators who won the cash-in, cash-out network on the street. The interesting question in 2026 is not whether Nigerian fintech is large. It is who owns the next layer.
$214M
Equity raised by Nigerian startups in H1 2026, the most of any African country (Africa: The Big Deal)
15.7B
Point-of-sale transactions in Nigeria in 2025, up 19.8% (Central Bank of Nigeria 2025 Annual Report)
$21.8B
Diaspora remittances into Nigeria in 2025, flat on 2024 (CBN data reported by Vanguard)
The Players
The market map, company by company
The four names that dominate Nigerian consumer and merchant fintech share one feature: each built or bought physical distribution. A Nigerian payments brand wins on the street, through agents and terminals in shops, before it wins in an app store. The figures below are the latest publicly reported, with the date and source for each.
OPay IPO talk
Valuation ~$3.1B implied (Opera filing, Apr 2026)
Last priced round $400M at ~$2B, SoftBank, 2021
Scale 50M+ users, 500k+ agents
Next step US listing near $4B reported
Moniepoint Unicorn
Valuation $1B+ (Oct 2024), no new figure since
Series C $200M total, closed Oct 2025
Backers DPI, LeapFrog, IFC, Google, Visa
Licence National MFB, Jan 2026
PalmPay Raising
Valuation Above $1B in talks (Bloomberg, Aug 2026)
Round ~$200M under discussion
Scale 40M+ users (Sep 2025)
Next step Hong Kong listing explored
Kuda Restructuring
Valuation $500M (Series B, 2021)
2024 loss $5.83M, down 84%
Customers 7M registered (2024)
2026 Layoffs in March
Sources: The Condia and WeeTracker on Opera's filing (Apr 2026); ThisDay citing Bloomberg (May 2026); TechCabal and Techpoint (Oct 2025); Bloomberg (Aug 2026); Nairametrics (Sep 2025); BusinessDay on Kuda's audited accounts (Jan 2026).
OPay: the largest network, priced through a shareholder
OPay has not raised a priced round since 2021, when SoftBank's Vision Fund 2 led a $400 million round at about $2 billion. Its most useful valuation signal is indirect: Opera, which holds 9.7%, valued that stake at $294.6 million in an April 2026 securities filing, which implies roughly $3.1 billion for the whole company. Bloomberg has since reported that OPay is working with Citigroup, Deutsche Bank and JPMorgan on a possible US listing at around $4 billion. That is a report, not a filing, and should be read as such.
The operating scale behind the number is real: more than 50 million users in Nigeria, monthly transaction volume reported above $12 billion, and an agent network of more than 500,000. OPay reportedly reached its first monthly profit in 2024.
Moniepoint: the merchant terminal company that became a bank
Moniepoint crossed a $1 billion valuation in October 2024 on a $110 million first close of its Series C, led by Development Partners International with Google's Africa Investment Fund among the investors. A $90 million extension in October 2025 brought the Series C to $200 million, with LeapFrog anchoring the close and IFC, Visa, Proparco and Swedfund participating. No new valuation was disclosed.
Its own 2025 review describes more than 6 million businesses served and claims that 8 in 10 in-person payments in Nigeria run on a Moniepoint terminal. Revenue figures for 2025 circulate in a range from about $265 million to $600 million, but none is audited and we do not repeat them as fact. In August 2026 the company began phasing out its UK remittance product to refocus on Nigeria and Kenya, where it completed a 78% stake in a microfinance bank.
PalmPay: the handset-backed challenger
PalmPay's distinctive asset is its shareholder base: Transsion, maker of the Tecno, Infinix and itel phones that dominate the African handset market, alongside NetEase and MediaTek. It reported more than 40 million users in September 2025 and was ranked the top fintech in the Financial Times list of Africa's fastest-growing companies that year. In August 2026 Bloomberg reported it was in talks to raise around $200 million at a valuation above $1 billion and preparing for a possible Hong Kong listing. The round had not closed at the time of the report.
Kuda: the neobank that chose profitability
Kuda was the poster child of Nigerian digital banking in 2021, valued at $500 million after a $55 million Series B. Its audited 2024 accounts tell the story of the years since. The loss fell 84% to $5.83 million, operating expenses fell 61%, and registered customers grew to 7 million. Revenue in dollars fell 15%, while revenue at its Nigerian subsidiary nearly doubled in naira. The company restructured again with layoffs in March 2026.
Kuda's naira revenue nearly doubled in 2024 while its dollar revenue fell 15%. That single line explains most Nigerian fintech valuations.
The rest of the map
Beyond the four consumer leaders, the infrastructure layer is consolidating. Flutterwave raised a Series E in June 2026 at a reported $3.2 billion with Ripple among the investors, and acquired the open banking company Mono. Paystack , owned by Stripe, reorganised under a holding company after reaching group profitability and became a microfinance bank in January 2026. Paga reported $11 billion processed across 169 million transactions in 2025 and became PayPal's entry point into Nigeria. LemFi raised a $53 million Series B in January 2025 for diaspora remittances. Interswitch , valued at $1 billion when Visa took a stake in 2019, still has no listing date.
The Money
How much capital is going into Nigerian fintech
Funding trackers count differently, so their totals should never be compared with each other, only within the same series. On Partech's count, Nigerian startups raised $520 million in equity in 2024, up 11%, across 103 deals, the most of any African country. On Africa: The Big Deal's count, Nigeria raised $254 million in total in the first half of 2026, second to Egypt, but led the continent on equity with $214 million.
Across Africa as a whole, Partech counted $4.1 billion raised in 2025, up 25%, with fintech at $1.49 billion. Fintech remains the single largest category on every tracker, at around 40% of African startup funding.
The Currency
Why every dollar valuation in Nigeria needs a footnote
The official naira rate moved from about ₦462 per dollar in June 2023 to ₦1,535 at the end of 2024, a loss of roughly 70% of its dollar value in eighteen months. It recovered partially to about ₦1,450 at the end of 2025 and around ₦1,332 in early October 2026.
For a company that earns in naira and is valued in dollars, that is the dominant variable. A business can double its local revenue and still report a decline to a foreign investor, which is exactly what Kuda's accounts show. It also explains why the leaders that held their valuations are the ones with the largest transaction volumes, where scale outran the currency, and why several have built dollar-earning lines such as remittances. Any valuation comparison across 2021, 2024 and 2026 is partly a currency comparison.
The Regulator
What changed in regulation between 2024 and 2026
Identity enforcement From March 2024 the Central Bank of Nigeria required every account and wallet to be linked to a Bank Verification Number or National Identification Number, with unlinked accounts restricted.
The onboarding freeze Between 29 April and 3 June 2024 the CBN stopped OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, PalmPay and Paga from onboarding new customers until they tightened address and facial verification and blocked peer-to-peer crypto transfers.
National licences In January 2026 the same five were upgraded to national microfinance licences covering all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. Supervision now looks much more like bank supervision.
Bank recapitalisation New minimum capital for commercial banks, announced in March 2024, carried a 31 March 2026 deadline. The banks that complete it will be better capitalised competitors and partners for fintechs.
Open banking Nigeria issued Africa's first open banking operational guidelines in 2023. The planned August 2025 go-live slipped, and the CBN set out a phased rollout through 2026. Whether the rail is fully live should be checked at the time of reading.
The Opportunity
What is still unsolved
The 2023 EFInA Access to Financial Services survey found 64% of Nigerian adults formally financially included, up from 56% in 2020, and 26% fully excluded, roughly 40 million adults. The urban-rural gap was still 20 percentage points.
That remaining population is the hardest to reach with the model that won the first round. Agent networks need cash logistics, terminals need power and a data signal, and app-based products need a smartphone with data. The next layer of growth in Nigeria is likely to come from products that keep working when one of those inputs is missing, and from distribution that does not assume a city.
Where We Sit
MobiBank and Nigeria
MobiBank is a Finnish financial technology company building a mobile banking platform for markets where connectivity and infrastructure cannot be assumed, including a patented channel that allows the service to work without internet access. Nigeria is the first market in our Africa rollout, and we have published our partnership and deployment plans on this site.
MobiBank is not yet licensed in Nigeria and does not offer accounts there today. Certain capabilities described across this site remain under development, and the licensing route is still being finalised.
Common Questions
Frequently asked questions
What is the biggest fintech company in Nigeria?
By users and implied valuation, OPay. Its shareholder Opera valued its 9.7% stake at $294.6 million in April 2026, implying about $3.1 billion, and OPay reports more than 50 million users in Nigeria and over 500,000 agents. Moniepoint is the largest by merchant payments, claiming that 8 in 10 in-person payments in Nigeria run on its terminals. Flutterwave, reported at $3.2 billion in June 2026, is the largest in business payments infrastructure.
What is OPay's valuation in 2026?
About $3.1 billion on an implied basis. Opera disclosed in an April 2026 filing that its 9.7% stake was worth $294.6 million. OPay's last priced round was $400 million at around $2 billion in 2021. Bloomberg reported in 2026 that OPay is working with banks on a possible US listing at about $4 billion, which is a report rather than a filed offering.
What is Moniepoint's valuation?
The public figure is above $1 billion, set when Moniepoint became a unicorn in October 2024 on the first close of its Series C. A $90 million extension in October 2025 brought the Series C to $200 million, with investors including DPI, LeapFrog, IFC, Google and Visa, but no updated valuation was disclosed.
Is PalmPay going public?
It is reported to be preparing. In August 2026 Bloomberg reported that PalmPay was in talks to raise around $200 million at a valuation above $1 billion and was exploring a Hong Kong listing, with no banks or timetable set. PalmPay is backed by Transsion, NetEase and MediaTek and reported more than 40 million users in September 2025.
Is Kuda Bank profitable?
Not on a full-year basis in its latest audited accounts. Kuda's 2024 loss was $5.83 million, down 84% from $35.11 million in 2023, after operating expenses were cut by 61%. Revenue at its Nigerian subsidiary nearly doubled in naira while group revenue fell 15% in dollars because of the currency. Full-year 2025 results had not been published at the time of writing.
How much did Nigerian fintech startups raise in 2025 and 2026?
It depends on the tracker. Partech counted $520 million of equity into Nigerian startups in 2024, the most in Africa. Africa: The Big Deal counted $254 million into Nigerian startups in the first half of 2026, with $214 million of that as equity, again the most in Africa. Fintech accounts for roughly 40% of African startup funding on every major tracker. Figures from different trackers use different methods and should not be compared directly.
Is Nigeria a good market for fintech investment?
It is the largest and most competitive fintech market in Africa, with deep demand and a regulator that has become stricter and more bank-like since 2024. The main risks are currency, since the naira lost roughly 70% of its dollar value between mid-2023 and end-2024, and regulatory change. The main opportunity is the roughly 40 million adults still financially excluded, who are hardest to reach with app-only and terminal-dependent models. This is general information, not investment advice.
What licences do Nigerian fintechs need?
It depends on the activity. Consumer players that hold deposits typically operate as microfinance banks, and in January 2026 the Central Bank of Nigeria upgraded OPay, Moniepoint, Kuda, PalmPay and Paga to national microfinance licences covering the whole country. Payments-only businesses use payment service licences, and agent networks fall under the CBN's agent banking guidelines. Every account must be linked to a BVN or NIN.

Navigating Nigerian Fintech Regulations: CBN, SEC, and NDIC Licensing Guide
Articles
Introduction
A Nigerian fintech startup rarely answers to a single regulator. Depending on whether a platform moves money, holds customer balances, issues investment products, or trades digital assets, it may need to satisfy the Central Bank of Nigeria (“CBN”), the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”), and the Nigeria Deposit Insurance Corporation (“NDIC”) often simultaneously. Each authority enforces distinct licensing categories, capital thresholds, and compliance schedules. These boundaries have shifted substantially following the Investment and Securities Act 2025 (“ISA 2025”) and recent regulatory circulars.
This guide maps the regulatory terrain for founders, investors, and in-house legal counsel structuring or scaling a Nigerian fintech entity.
The CBN Pathway: Payments and Deposit-Taking
Licensing Categories Under the CBN’s updated framework, the principal non-bank payment licences include:
Payment Solution Service Provider (PSSP): Covers payment gateways, processing, and merchant integration. A PSSP cannot hold customer funds or issue wallets, making it an ideal entry point for early-stage processing startups.
Mobile Money Operator (MMO): Permits operators to hold and move customer funds using pooled/trust accounts at deposit money banks and to issue e-wallets.
Payment Terminal Service Provider (PTSP): Covers the deployment and maintenance of point-of-sale (POS) infrastructure.
Switching and Processing: Covers settlement and routing infrastructure connecting banks, processors, and payment channels.
Super-Agent: Regulates agent networks delivering agency-banking services on behalf of licensed institutions.
Payment Service Bank (PSB): Focuses on financial inclusion. PSBs can take deposits and offer payment services, but cannot extend loans or deal in foreign exchange.
Capital requirements vary considerably. Switching and Processing licences carry a minimum paid-up capital requirement of ₦2 billion, while MMO and PSB thresholds sit at or above ₦5 billion.
Critical Distinction: Minimum paid-up share capital is distinct from the refundable escrow deposit lodged with the CBN during application. Conflating these two figures is a common and costly budgeting error for early-stage startups.
The Application Process
The CBN application follows five key stages:
Name reservation and incorporation with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC).
Formal application submission including business plans, governance policies, and capital verification.
Issuance of an Approval-in-Principle (AIP) .
System build-out, integration testing, and on-site CBN inspection.
Issuance of the Final Licence .
Note: An AIP is strictly an authorization to build and test systems, it does NOT authorize an operator to onboard paying customers or process live transactions.
The SEC Pathway: Investment, Crowdfunding, and Digital Assets
When a Fintech Needs SEC Registration
A fintech that limits itself to payment processing will typically stay within the CBN’s perimeter. The moment a product touches investment products, pooled retail capital, algorithm-driven financial advice, or virtual or digital assets, however, the SEC’s jurisdiction is engaged often in parallel with, rather than instead of, any CBN requirement.
Crowdfunding Intermediaries
Investment-based crowdfunding is regulated under the SEC’s Rules on Crowdfunding, first issued in January 2021 and now operating within the expanded framework of ISA 2025 [1] . Any platform through which a fundraiser offers investment instruments to the public must be a registered Crowdfunding Intermediary, and the portal itself must separately register with the SEC. Registration requirements are substantial: certified incorporation documents, audited accounts, an operational manual, minimum capital, a fidelity bond, and SEC-sponsored individuals within the governance structure.
Robo-Advisory Services
Automated, algorithm-driven investment platforms fall within the SEC’s Rules on Robo-Advisory Services, issued in August 2021 [2] . A Robo-Adviser must satisfy the same business-conduct standards applicable to human-supervised investment advisers regulated by the SEC, and its principal officers must demonstrate relevant experience in both financial management and the underlying technology. Where the platform advises on foreign securities, it must additionally put risk-mitigation mechanisms in place for investors, and it must disclose to clients in writing the assumptions and limitations built into its algorithms and the circumstances in which the operator may override or suspend the automated advice.
Virtual and Digital Assets
ISA 2025 makes the most consequential change to this landscape, it expressly brings digital assets, smart contracts, and tokenised securities within the statutory definition of “securities,” and creates dedicated licence categories for Virtual Asset Service Providers and related digital-asset operators [3] . This resolves at least on paper the jurisdictional grey zone that previously existed between the CBN and SEC over crypto-related activity. Virtual asset business is now unambiguously an SEC-regulated activity, subject to registration, capital, and disclosure obligations applicable to other regulated capital market operators.
A related SEC circular on revised minimum capital requirements, applicable to Virtual Asset Service Providers and to fintech operators generally, increased capital thresholds for several existing licence categories and introduced new thresholds for newly created digital-asset categories [4] .
The NDIC Touchpoint: Deposit Insurance for Fintech Customers
The NDIC does not licence fintechs. Its relevance arises because many CBN-licensed fintechs particularly Mobile Money Operators do not hold customer funds directly in their own name, but instead maintain pooled or trust accounts at a partner deposit money bank on behalf of subscribers. The NDIC extends protection to the underlying subscribers of that pool through the Pass-Through Deposit Insurance scheme [5] . Rather than insuring the pool account as a single lump sum, the NDIC looks through the account to the individual subscriber balances it contains and insures each subscriber separately, up to the applicable coverage limit.
Coverage levels have been revised upward periodically and, as at the NDIC’s most recent general increase, stand at ₦5,000,000 per subscriber for Mobile Money Operator pool accounts aligned with the coverage level for deposit money bank customers and ₦2,000,000 per depositor for Payment Service Banks and Microfinance Banks [6] . These figures matter to a fintech’s commercial proposition and disclosure obligations: subscriber-facing terms and marketing materials that overstate or understate the coverage actually available expose the operator to both regulatory and consumer-protection risk.
For a startup structuring its banking relationships, the practical point is that pass-through insurance is only available where the underlying pool or trust account arrangement meets the NDIC’s structural requirements including a properly documented bare trust relationship between the operator and its subscribers, and a pool account held at an NDIC-insured deposit money bank. A fintech that structures its custody arrangements loosely, or routes customer funds through an unlicensed intermediary, risks its subscribers falling outside the pass-through scheme entirely, regardless of how the product is marketed.
Sequencing the Pathway: A Practical Framework
The three regulatory touchpoints are not encountered simultaneously in practice, and startups that treat them as a single undifferentiated “licensing project” tend to over-engineer their early compliance spend. A more workable sequence is as follows.
Start with the Core Function : Identify the single activity that defines the minimum viable product, payment processing, wallet issuance, investment access, or asset custody and secure the licence that activity actually requires before building adjacent features. Most early-stage payments startups will find a PSSP licence sufficient at launch, notwithstanding the temptation to apply for a broader category in anticipation of future functionality.
Treat Product Expansion as a Licensing Trigger : Each new feature should be screened against the CBN and SEC perimeters before development begins, not after launch. A savings feature that begins pooling customer funds may convert a PSSP-appropriate business into one that requires an MMO licence; an investment or “round-up and invest” feature will very likely trigger SEC registration, whether as a Robo-Adviser, a crowdfunding intermediary, or otherwise, depending on how the product is structured.
Confirm the Deposit Insurance Position Early, Not at Crisis Point : Where a product relies on pooled customer funds, the banking partner, the account structure, and the trust documentation should be settled and the pass-through insurance position confirmed before the product is marketed to consumers. Subscriber-facing claims about fund safety should be reviewed by counsel against the actual structural position, not against a general assumption that “the funds are insured.”
Budget for Two Kinds of Capital : Founders raising a seed or Series A round to fund licensing should distinguish, in their capital planning, between paid-up share capital (which supports the balance sheet and is not readily recoverable) and refundable escrow or bond deposits (which are recoverable but tie up working capital for the duration of the licence’s life). Conflating the two in a cap table or investor deck is a recurring and avoidable diligence flag.
Common Pitfalls
Applying for a licence category broader than the current product requires, and carrying capital and compliance overhead the business is not yet generating revenue to support.
Treating an Approval-in-Principle as authorisation to onboard paying customers or move live funds.
Adding a savings, investment, or crypto-adjacent feature without first screening it against SEC registration requirements.
Marketing “fund safety” or “insured deposits” to consumers without confirming that the underlying account structure actually qualifies for NDIC pass-through coverage.
Underestimating the ongoing compliance burden transaction monitoring, sanctions screening, and fraud-liability obligations relative to the one-off cost of obtaining the licence itself.
Conclusion
The regulatory pathway for a Nigerian fintech is not a single door but a sequence of doors, each opened by a different regulator in response to what the product actually does. The CBN governs the movement and custody of money, the SEC increasingly governs where that money is invested or tokenised, and the NDIC quietly underwrites the safety net beneath both. Startups that map their product roadmap against all three regulators from the outset rather than discovering a second or third licensing obligation after launch will find the pathway considerably shorter, and considerably less expensive, than those that do not.

Top Fintechs in Nigeria of 2025
These fintechs, which include OPay, PiggyVest and Moniepoint, are leaders in their respective verticals, transforming payments, personal banking, investment and more.
Fintechnews Africa 3 October 2025 10 Mins Read
Share LinkedIn Facebook Twitter Telegram Copy Link Email
Share LinkedIn Facebook Twitter Telegram Copy Link Email
Free Newsletter
Subscribe to the most important Fintech News Africa
Nigeria, Africa’s biggest economy, is the driving force behind the continent’s fintech revolution. The country accounts for 28% of all African fintech companies and is a leading hub for venture capital (VC) funding, capturing the highest share of fintech funding in African fintech companies between 2020 and H1 2024 at roughly 36%.
This rapidly growing ecosystem, which now comprises more than 430 fintech companies, also hosts some of the continent’s most prominent and influential players in the industry.
Today, we take a look at Nigeria’s top fintechs, showcasing the country’s most impactful fintech companies, highlighting their value propositions, and delving into their recent milestones.
For this list, we focus on private, independent fintech companies based in Nigeria, excluding the likes of Flutterwave, which is headquartered in the US, and Kuda Bank, based in London. We also exclude those that have been acquired or which are affiliated with major banks, telecom providers, or established entities, such as Paystack ( acquired by PayPal in 2020), and MoMo Payment Service, a subsidiary of MTN Nigeria Communications. This approach aims to provide a clear view of Nigeria’s homegrown fintech trailblazers.
Top fintechs in Nigeria
OPay
OPay illustration, Source: OPay Established in 2018, OPay is a leading fintech company from Nigeria providing financial services to consumers and merchants across Africa and Asia. The company offers a one-stop financial service platform for payments, transfers, savings, loans and other essential consumers services, as well as point-of-sale (POS) services for agents, and acquiring services for merchant.
With a strong presence in Nigeria, Egypt, and Pakistan, OPay has rapidly expanded. In April 2024, the company claimed over 50 million users and 1 million merchants, 10 million daily active trading users, and monthly transaction volumes surpassing US$12 billion. It has also had a significant impact, fostering 400,000 direct and indirect job opportunities.
Last year, OPay achieved its first monthly profit.
Its growth and performance has also garnered international media attention and industry recognition, with features in Forbes, CNN, CB Insights’ Global Fintech 250 list for three consecutive years, as well as the CNBC’s 2023 Global Fintech 200 ranking.
OPay has also secured major investments, including a US$120 million Series B in 2019 and a US$400 million Series C in 2021, valuing the company at US$2 billion.
Looking ahead, the company aims to expand its reach in its existing markets of Egypt and Pakistan, while also venturing into new countries and regions. The company’s vision is to serve 1 billion users and 10 million merchants, ultimately creating 3 million job opportunities by 2031.
Interswitch
Interswitch illustration, Source: Interswitch Founded in 2002, Interswitch is a Nigerian-founded digital payments and commerce company. Originally established as a transaction switching and electronic payments processor, the company has evolved into an integrated payments services provider, building infrastructure and delivering innovative, omni-channel payment solutions across the continent.
With a stronghold in Nigeria and growing influence across Africa, Interswitch supports over 8,000 billers via its Quickteller platform, enables more than 41,000 Quickteller Paypoint agents, and facilitates daily transactions for over 190,000 active businesses. Its Verve card network, meanwhile, has surpassed 70 million activated cards. Quickteller is a multi-channel payments platform, while Verve is a Pan-African chip and PIN payment card solution.
Interswitch’s rapid growth has attracted significant investor interest, with over US$300 million raised to date, including a US$200 million Visa-led round.
Interswitch has considered going public multiple times, but these plans have been postponed due to various economic factors and market conditions. As of now, the company remains privately held. However, in 2020, it listed a NGN 23 billion (US$63.3 million) bond on the Nigerian Stock Exchange as part of a NGN 30 billion (US$82.5 billion) debt issuance program.
Cowrywise
Cowrywise mockup, Source: Cowrywise Founded in 2017, Cowrywise is an investment company and wealth manager that aims to democratize access to savings and investment products for the underserved African middle class and millennials.
Licensed by the Nigerian Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the company provides a platform that digitizes investment management, offering tools that allow individuals to save and invest on their own terms and build better financial habits. These tools include goal-based savings, easy access to secure investment products, real-time tracking of their net worth, as well as features such as Sprout for business treasury management, and Triggers for automated, event-based investing.
Cowrywise claims more than 1,000,000 users, making it a prominent wealthtech startup in Nigeria. The startup was the first Nigerian company to be accepted into Catalyst Fund program, backed by JP Morgan and UKAID, and is also an Y Combinator alumnus.
It has received backing from prominent investors including Quona Capital, Venture Souq, SHL Capital, and Kairos 50 Ventures, and has earned a number of accolades, including being named one of the Top 10 Startups in Nigeria in 2022, as well as one of the best apps made in Nigeria in 2022.
Paga
Paga platforms, Source: Paga Founded in early 2009, Paga aims to deliver innovative and universal access to financial services in Africa. Licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), Paga operates a secure and flexible payments platform accessible via basic mobile phones, smartphones, online channels, and a widespread agent network. It enables users to send money to any phone number, make deposits to bank accounts, pay bills, and perform cardless ATM withdrawals.
For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), Paga provides a suite of payment solutions that allows merchants to collect debit card or mobile money payments securely. The company claims its platform-as-a-service (PaaS) solution to used by over 150 businesses.
As of 2024, Paga had processed over 335 million transactions totaling NGN 14 trillion (US$32 billion), and served 23 million users, underscoring the startup’s position as a key platform in Nigeria’s digital payments landscape.
Last year, Paga was recognized in the Financial Times Africa’s Fastest Growing Companies special report, highlighting its remarkable growth and journey.
FairMoney
FairMoney loans illustration, Source: FairMoney Founded in 2017, FairMoney is building a leading mobile bank for emerging markets, focusing on providing accessible, tech-driven financial services to the underbanked.
Licensed by the CBN as a microfinance bank, FairMoney offers neobanking solutions including current accounts, savings, lending, deposits, peer-to-peer (P2P) payments, bill payments, POS payment acceptance, investments, and business solutions, amongst many other disruptive services.
With over 17 million app downloads, 5 million users , and 10,000 daily loan disbursements, FairMoney is considered one of the fastest-growing companies in Africa. The startup is backed by some of the most prominent fintech investors like DST, TLcom Capital, newfund, Flourish Ventures, SpeedInvest, and Tiger Global.
Moniepoint
Moniepoint point-of-sale (POS) system, Source: Moniepoint Founded in 2015, Moniepoint, formerly known as TeamApt, is building an all-in-one financial platform. The company provides services spanning POS terminals, business accounts, and payment processing solutions to help businesses manage their operations, accept payments, and access credit. It also serves personal banking solutions, allowing users to make transfers, pay bills and buy airtime, and more.
Moniepoint claims to serve more than 10 million businesses and individuals. It also says it is one of Nigeria’s largest merchant acquirers, powering most of the country’s POS transactions. The startup processes over 1 billion transactions monthly, with total payments volume exceeding US$22 billion.
Moniepoint reached unicorn status in October 2024 following a US$110 million funding round . In January 2025, the startup secured an investment from Visa to further accelerate its growth and expansion across the continent. This partnership aims to support Moniepoint’s continental expansion and enhance transaction visibility through Visa’s Cybersource system. Additionally, the company plans to integrate with Visa Direct for remittances and money transfers as it looks to expand into markets within and outside Africa.
PalmPay
PalmPay mockup, Source: PalmPay Launched in 2018, PalmPay is a leading Africa-focused fintech platform committed to driving economic empowerment in Africa. Through its secure, user-friendly, and inclusive suite of financial services, PalmPay brings top-tier products into the pockets of everyday Nigerians, offering money transfers, bill payments, credit services, and savings on its app as well as via its expansive network of over 500,000 mobile money agents.
In addition to personal banking services, PalmPay also provides a suite of business-to-business (B2B) offerings for local micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) and international merchants. These services include smart POS terminals and a business app, payment orchestration and checkout solutions, bulk payment tools via a self-service merchant portal, and application programming interfaces (APIs) for embedding and reselling PalmPay’s services.
Since launching in Nigeria under a mobile money operator license, PalmPay has grown its customer base to over 35 million registered users and more than 600,000 merchants. The startup has also expanded to new markets, establishing operations in Tanzania, Ghana, and Bangladesh. It claims to process up to 15 million transactions daily.
Recently, PalmPay was recognized as one of the World’s Top 250 Fintech Companies in 2024 by CNBC and Statista, further underscoring its position as a major player in Nigeria’s fintech ecosystem.
PiggyVest
PiggyVest Flex Naira illustration, Source: PiggyVest Originally launched as Piggybank.ng as a savings-only platform in 2016, the platform rebranded to PiggyVest in April 2019 to offer direct investment opportunities to users in addition to savings.
Today, PiggyVest offers a range of financial tools including automated savings, fixed savings, target-based savings, Flex Naira/Dollar accounts, and group savings for rent and household expenses. These tools allow users to customize their savings journey to match their goals, whether they are saving daily, weekly, or monthly.
PiggyVest claims 5 million users. In January 2025, the startup hit a major milestone, reaching NGN 2 trillion (US$1.25 billion) in total payouts to users since inception, with NGN 835 billion (US$547.3 million) paid out in 2024 alone, representing a 53% YoY increase. It also reported a 76% increase in assets under management (AUM).
In 2024, PiggyVest was recognized among the world’s top 250 fintech companies by CNBC, underscoring its innovative approach to financial planning and its significant role in shaping the future of finance.
Looking ahead, the startup plans to expand its offerings further. In particular, it will introduce a budgeting feature aimed at helping users manage daily expenses and ensure their salaries last until the next payday. PiggyVest has also hinted at potential plans for an Initial Public Offering (IPO) in the future.
Nomba
Nomba mockup, Source: Nomba Founded in 2016, Nomba, formerly known as Kudi, aims to simplify financial services for businesses and individuals across Africa. Initially launched as a chatbot that responds to financial requests, allowing users to make transfers, buy airtime, and pay bills, the company quickly pivoted to agency banking services, adding payments and business banking services for its users.
Today, Nomba offers a payment platform and mobile wallet that facilitate digital transactions, allowing individuals and merchants to send and receive money, make payments for goods and services, and manage their finances from a mobile device.
As of May 2023, the company served more than 300,000 businesses and processed US$1 billion in monthly transactions.
In April, it announced a partnership with Mastercard to integrate Mastercard Gateway into Nomba Checkout, enabling businesses to process payments seamlessly, securely, and efficiently, both locally and globally. The startup also plans to expand its payment offerings, supporting multiple transaction methods, including international cards and QR codes.
