E-Financial CBN Warns Banks, Fintechs on Compliance with Sanctions
Comms Week 18 Apr 2025 0 Comments
Kindly share this post Copy Link
Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has reminded banks, payment service banks, and fintech companies of their obligations to comply with applicable sanctions regimes. These sanctions include the United…
Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has reminded banks, payment service banks, and fintech companies of their obligations to comply with applicable sanctions regimes.
These sanctions include the United Nations Consolidated Sanctions List, the Nigerian Sanctions List in line with the Terrorism (Prevention and Prohibition) Act 2022, and guidelines on targeted financial sanctions related to terrorism and its financing.
This was contained in a letter dated April 17, 2025 and signed by Amonia Opusunju for the director of the Compliance Department.
The CBN directed all financial institutions to ensure strict adherence to sanctions lists maintained at both international and national levels.
According to the apex bank, financial institutions are expected to regularly update their systems to identify designated persons or entities and prevent the misuse of financial platforms to facilitate illegal transactions.
The letter read: “Financial Institutions are required to maintain a robust and dynamic sanctions compliance framework that enables them to Identify and respond promptly to updates or changes across all applicable sanctions lists; Prevent the use of their systems and platforms for transactions involving designated individuals or entities; Conduct real-time screening of customers, transactions, and beneficial owners; and File appropriate reports with the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) and notify the CBN, where necessary.”
The CBN’s directive also covers real-time screening of customers, transactions, and beneficial owners.
Institutions are to report suspicious activities to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU) and notify the apex bank where necessary, the apex bank warned.
According to the bank, non-compliance with the regulations could attract sanctions in form of enforcement actions or regulatory penalties.
It added that sanctions compliance frameworks must be periodically reviewed and aligned with prevailing laws and regulatory expectations.
The CBN advised all financial institutions to take note of the guidance and act accordingly.
“This letter serves as a regulatory reminder and all Financial Institutions are expected to ensure continued compliance with applicable laws and CBN directives,” the apex bank stated.

Introduction to Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) plays a pivotal role in regulating payments and financial institutions across Nigeria. For merchants seeking merchant identification number (MID) onboarding and payment service providers (PSPs) pursuing licensing or compliance, CBN licensing requirements are essential to navigate the Nigerian payments landscape.
Whether you are launching new payment services or expanding operations in Nigeria, understanding CBN’s regulatory framework is crucial. This multi-sector regulator oversees monetary policy, payment systems, and banking compliance, directly impacting your market entry, operational legality, and risk management strategies in the Nigerian payments ecosystem.
This guide outlines the jurisdiction and scope of the Central Bank of Nigeria, details the relevant payment licenses, explains the licensing process, and highlights compliance obligations. You’ll find practical advice on avoiding common pitfalls, managing regulatory risks, and meeting CBN’s expectations to ensure smooth merchant onboarding and PSP compliance.
How to identify valid CBN licenses for PSPs in Nigeria
Which requirements affect merchant onboarding under CBN rules
Key compliance standards to maintain good standing with CBN
Practical tips for navigating regulatory risks in Nigerian payments
Jurisdiction & Scope of Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) serves as the principal monetary authority in Nigeria, regulating key aspects of the financial sector that directly impact payment services. Understanding the CBN jurisdiction is vital for any PSP or merchant looking to operate legally within Nigeria’s complex payments ecosystem.
The CBN oversees a broad multi-sector scope, including the regulation of banks, payment service providers (PSPs), and payment systems infrastructure. It enforces compliance with financial stability, consumer protection, and anti-money laundering standards. Both local and foreign entities offering payment solutions or financial services in Nigeria fall under its supervision, making it a central gatekeeper for seamless and secure money transmission regulation in the country.
Key areas under CBN oversight:
Regulation of Nigerian banks and financial institutions
Licensing and supervision of payment service providers (PSPs)
Oversight of payment systems and electronic funds transfers
Enforcement of consumer protection in financial services
Oversight of money transmission activities within Nigeria
Takeaway for merchants & PSPs: To serve the Nigerian market, PSPs must obtain the appropriate licenses from the CBN, while merchants should partner only with CBN-authorized payment providers.
Regulated Entities under Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) regulates a broad range of financial entities including money transmitters, state-licensed banks, and payment service providers (PSPs), ensuring safe and reliable payment systems for Nigerian businesses and consumers. Understanding which entities require CBN licensing is crucial for merchants selecting PSPs and for PSPs entering the Nigerian market.
CBN’s regulatory scope covers money transmission companies, commercial and specialized banks, microfinance banks, lenders, fintech startups, and stored value issuers operating within Nigeria. Entities with a physical presence must satisfy local compliance mandates, including obtaining the necessary licenses and maintaining registered offices. Foreign PSPs or payment providers offering services to Nigerian residents are also subject to CBN licensing and supervisory requirements, regardless of physical location, to protect the integrity of Nigeria’s payment ecosystem.
Entities regulated by Central Bank of Nigeria include:
Money Transmission Companies (MTCs) handling payments for Nigerian residents
State-chartered commercial and microfinance banks operating in Nigeria
Payment Service Providers (PSPs) facilitating merchant payment acceptance
Fintech companies offering lending or stored value services within Nigeria
Foreign-based PSPs serving Nigerian customers through local partnerships or platforms
Local Presence Requirements:
Most regulated entities must maintain a registered office in Nigeria and appoint a local compliance officer or agent to liaise with CBN and ensure adherence to ongoing supervisory obligations.
Implications for Foreign PSPs:
Payment providers headquartered outside Nigeria but servicing Nigerian residents must secure appropriate licensing from CBN and comply with Nigerian regulatory standards before offering services.
What Merchants Should Know:
Merchants should work exclusively with payment providers licensed by CBN to ensure compliance and reduce exposure to regulatory risks when processing payments within Nigeria.
Licenses Overview under Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)

Licensing Process with Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) enforces a rigorous licensing process for payment service providers in Nigeria. Early preparation of robust corporate, financial, and compliance materials is critical to navigating the regulatory requirements efficiently and ensuring a timely application outcome.
Step-by-Step Application
Pre-Application Preparation – compile audited financial statements, detailed compliance manuals including AML/KYC policies, and designate a local representative or agent.
Application Submission – complete CBN’s official licensing forms, submit proof of the required surety bond, and pay the applicable application fees.
Background Checks & Review – the CBN evaluates the integrity and expertise of the management team along with the company’s capital adequacy and operational plans.
Approval & License Issuance – upon meeting all regulatory prerequisites, CBN issues the license and sets conditions for ongoing compliance.
Post-Issuance Compliance – maintain regular reporting, adhere strictly to AML/KYC obligations, and uphold consumer protection standards as mandated by the CBN.
⏳ Timelines & Costs at a Glance
Average review duration: 90–120 days
Licensing fees: generally start from NGN 2,000,000 and vary by entity size and scope
Surety bond requirements: typically NGN 10,000,000+, depending on license type and business volume
Pro Insight:
Engage with CBN compliance officers early and ensure your AML/KYC frameworks are comprehensive and clearly documented to minimize review delays during the licensing process.
If you’re wondering how to apply for a Nigeria money transmitter license or want to understand the licensing process for payment providers fully, following these CBN application steps closely will greatly enhance your chances of success.
Compliance & Supervision by Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN)
Holding a license with the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) requires payment providers to meet ongoing compliance obligations beyond initial approval. Continuous adherence to these obligations is vital for securing long-term market access and building trust in Nigeria’s dynamic payments landscape.
Key Compliance Obligations
Maintain AML/KYC Frameworks – implement and regularly update anti-money laundering and know-your-customer procedures aligned with CBN’s federal standards.
Submit Regulatory Reports – deliver quarterly and annual financial statements and operational disclosures without delays.
File Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) – promptly report any suspicious or high-risk transactions as mandated by CBN guidelines.
Safeguard Consumer Funds – ensure client money is protected via escrow accounts or segregation mechanisms to prevent misuse.
Transparent Customer Disclosures – provide clear, accurate information on fees, terms, and risk to enhance consumer protection.
Maintain Required Capital & Bonds – uphold minimum capital levels and valid surety bonds as stipulated to mitigate financial risk.
Adhere to Data Security Standards – enforce robust cybersecurity protocols protecting payment data integrity and confidentiality.

CBN actively monitors Nigeria money transmitter supervision through these mechanisms. Non-compliance can lead to fines, license revocation, or operational restrictions, reinforcing the importance of continuous regulatory reporting requirements and internal controls.
Enforcement in Practice
The CBN has imposed penalties on licensed payment providers for failures such as lapses in AML controls and insufficient surety bond maintenance. These actions demonstrate the regulator’s commitment to maintaining a resilient and trustworthy payments ecosystem in Nigeria.
Expert Insight:
Providers that only treat payment provider compliance obligations as a checkbox exercise risk costly audits, regulatory sanctions, and reputational damage in Nigeria’s tightly supervised payment sector.
Merchant Relevance: What Central Bank of Nigeria Means for You
If you operate a business in Nigeria, working with a licensed PSP regulated by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) is crucial for compliant MID onboarding and secure merchant payment operations. While merchants don’t apply for licenses themselves, choosing a licensed PSP ensures your payment processes meet local regulatory standards, protecting you from financial and legal risks.
Key Implications for Merchants
☑️ Always select a PSP licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria to ensure full MID onboarding compliance and avoid regulatory pitfalls.
☑️ A CBN-licensed PSP guarantees your settlement funds are managed under strict consumer protection guidelines.
☑️ Licensed PSPs are subject to ongoing CBN supervision, which helps maintain merchant payment security and transaction integrity.
☑️ Partnering with a regulated provider reduces the risk of service disruptions caused by enforcement actions or sudden license revocation.
☑️ Verify license status regularly through the CBN registry to safeguard your business against the risk of unlicensed providers.
Red Flags to Avoid
PSPs not listed on the official Central Bank of Nigeria PSP registry.
Lack of transparent AML/KYC procedures or vague compliance commitments.
Hidden or unclear fees, and inconsistent or delayed settlement timelines.
Providers with a history of consumer complaints, penalties, or regulatory enforcement by the CBN.
✅ Merchant Takeaway: Always confirm your PSP is licensed by the Central Bank of Nigeria; it’s the simplest safeguard against compliance issues and protects your payment operations from avoidable risks.
PSP Relevance: Licensing & Compliance under Central Bank of Nigeria
For PSPs operating in Nigeria, securing a money transmitter license from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) is mandatory before offering any payment services to Nigerian residents. The CBN demands that providers demonstrate solid financial standing, maintain a surety bond, implement robust AML/KYC processes, and fulfill comprehensive reporting duties. This section offers practical guidance on navigating PSP licensing requirements in Nigeria, ensuring compliance from application through ongoing operations.
Licensing Obligations
Obtain a CBN money transmitter license if you intend to serve customers within Nigeria.
Meet minimum capital requirements and furnish a surety bond in accordance with CBN regulations.
Designate a dedicated compliance officer or local representative based in Nigeria.
Submit detailed AML/KYC policies and risk management frameworks as part of your license application.
Provide audited financial statements, proof of operational readiness, and governance documentation.
Ongoing Compliance
File quarterly and annual financial reports along with suspicious activity reports (SARs) to the CBN.
Maintain continuous AML/KYC training programs tailored to Nigerian regulations for all relevant staff.
Report promptly any material changes in ownership, governance, or financial conditions.
Cooperate fully with CBN’s periodic audits and on-site examinations.
⚡ Maintaining open communication with the Central Bank of Nigeria and establishing a strong compliance framework will streamline renewals and support sustainable growth in the Nigerian payments market.
Risk & Red Flags in Nigeria
Navigating regulatory risks for payment providers in Nigeria requires careful attention to the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) stringent requirements. The CBN often denies license applications or imposes fines due to common licensing pitfalls that stem from incomplete documentation, weak compliance frameworks, or inaccurate disclosures. Early identification and mitigation of these risks are essential to avoid costly enforcement actions and protect your business reputation in Nigeria’s evolving payments ecosystem.
Common Pitfalls
Submitting incomplete or inaccurate financial disclosures, including audited statements.
Failure to maintain the required minimum net worth and surety bond as stipulated by CBN.
Weak AML/KYC controls exposing providers to money laundering and fraud risks.
Delays or failures in submitting mandatory periodic reports such as regulatory returns and suspicious activity reports (SARs).
Lack of a locally registered compliance officer or designated registered agent in Nigeria.
Misrepresentation or inconsistent disclosure of ownership structure and beneficial owners.
Non-compliance with consumer protection rules, including transaction transparency and dispute resolution protocols.
Market-Specific Risks: Nigeria imposes significant penalties for operating without a valid license, including criminal prosecution. The CBN also closely monitors cross-border and foreign currency payment transmissions, which increases the regulatory scrutiny on PSPs engaging in international transactions.
Bottom Line: Avoiding these red flags is critical for securing your license and maintaining regulatory trust in Nigeria.
